title: Memorial Sesshin, Mel Weitsman on How to Sit Zazen
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads Sojun Mel Weitsman's short essay on how to sit zazen, a photocopied Berkeley Zen Center newsletter piece, as a memorial offering during sesshin. Mel describes zazen as a balance of gravity and spirit, passive and active, and ends with the line "your shoulders don't hold you up." Nomon then takes up Dogen's "think not thinking" in Fukanzazengi and the Yaoshan koan behind it, drawing on Koun Franz's explanation that the Japanese shiryu means measuring, evaluative thought. Along the way Nomon tells of catching a sudden urge to check a phone and coming back to the breath. Nomon closes by breathing with Mel and Buddha, with no gaps.

sentences.text: Thanks, everybody.
I'm feeling really honored to get to speak with you this morning, so thanks in advance for sharing your attention with me.
Even over Zoom, talks are not just broadcasts; they're really co-created.
Speaker and sangha are interacting, supporting each other.
So thanks for that.
I really appreciated Norman's remarks yesterday about our dear colleague, Jay Semino, and about his teacher, Sojun Mel Weitsman's passing this year.
It's actually a normal thing in our tradition to have a memorial sesshin after an important teacher dies, so that's what we're doing this year, having a memorial sesshin for Mel.

I was thinking the spirit of this shouldn't only be to access whatever appreciation we might have, directly or indirectly, for Sojun Mel's practice: his incredible steadfastness, his hard work establishing a center and guiding others along the way, his unbelievable devotion to daily zazen, daily practice, showing up at the temple every day for 50, 60 years.
All that's wonderful, but it's like looking towards the past.
If we only did that, we'd be reducing Mel to nostalgia.
So the other important piece is to really inhabit our practice now.
That's the memorial sesshin: to show up now in our lives with the spirit inspired by this teacher and the many teachers.

I think a part of that might be, since we're doing a memorial sesshin for Sojun Mel Weitsman over Zoom, to be careful not to see the online sesshin as less than in any way, but as completely its own unique opportunity to practice.
I was thinking about this because when I was coming upstairs from breakfast to get ready for the talk, I was thinking about how my daily busy routine pulls me out of myself.
Do you know what I mean?
I was actually musing about this.
And then my mind jumped, as if on cue, to "where's my phone?"
It wasn't in my pocket.
It was a sesshin.
It took another half a second for my mind to imagine my phone sitting on the desk charging.
And in another half second I could feel, starting in the gut and emanating out to the limbs, this urge to go check.
I'm talking about not just a mental urge, but a physical, volitional thing.
I could feel my limbs start moving in that direction.
I was just grateful for the support of sesshin.
I don't think of myself as a serious smartphone addict, but it doesn't matter what I think.
Maybe I am.
But here's the support of our practice, to be able to drop back into the breathing, register that, let it go, and move on.
Sit down and follow my intention.
Just sit down and prepare the talk.
And the back story there is I've got enough going on with the organizations I support.
I'm not totally disconnected.
I'm checking crucial stuff, which is a slippery slope for sure, but also a great opportunity for practice.
So just try to fold your whole life, your everyday so-called ordinary life, into this sesshin, into this practice, in whatever way works for you.
That could be part of how we appreciate Mel and appreciate the Dharma, appreciate each other.
What a great opportunity, for this morning or this week, however long you're connected to all this, to feel into that support.
It's really here.
Dharma is really here.
Sangha is definitely here.
Here they are.
Support to take a fresh look, to do it differently, to see more possibilities and feel them.
Anyway, that was my little moment of practice that I thought I could honor Mel with.
I hope he appreciates it.
Maybe he'd chuckle with me, or maybe at me, about that.
I crossed paths with Mel mostly just for a couple of months, long ago at Green Gulch Farm, as a young man.
You made a big impression on me, like many of the Zen-worthies that I crossed paths with, and quite a few of them somehow.
I think at the time I was an interesting mix of starstruck and a bit skeptical.
My memory is not very complete about the past, very spotty; there's a lot I don't remember.

But the times I spent at the Residential Zen Center at Green Gulch Farm, back then at the tail end of my 20th year, 21 years old, and then I went back for a few months when I was 23, I think, so much from then is right there, very easy to access.
Different people and what they said and did, some of which I was amazed by, some of which I was disturbed by.
The rituals and forms of Zen, the place itself, down to all kinds of fine details.
I'm not that far from Green Gulch Farm right now where I'm sitting, but it's closed for the pandemic.
If I went there, I'd probably be a little confused, because it probably looks really different from these memories I have.
Maybe I'll just leave them be.
I remember poetry I wrote then; a whole little poem I wrote popped into my head this morning when I was thinking about this.
So it's really interesting: how does one time end up feeling more important than another time later in life?
There's something about our practice, maybe it helps us access the vividness of life.
I was also oddly comforted by Norman's words in a memorial about his teacher.
It's just so comforting that we have this form, a Dharma talk during sesshin, as a way of expressing this.
I was comforted about the reality that we will all lose our teachers, everyone, and that this is okay.
This is how it should be.
And this may sound a little morbid, but I actually found myself imagining myself 20 years from now as a 75-year-old, saying the same kinds of things in a future sesshin about Norman's passing.
Of course, who knows what will really happen, but it's a comfort, I think.
This sense we've received of lineage, and of practicing together for decades and decades.
Since I was down memory lane, I did the math: 35 years I've been practicing in this way with this teacher, with my teacher.
I'll be 55 in this imagined 20-years-from-now future.
But how comforting, the way the Dharma is passed from warm hand to warm hand, quietly, subtly, sometimes with a few fireworks, to be sure, but mostly pretty quiet and organic.
It's natural, like living and dying is also natural.
Everything arising and passing away just as it should.
Students become teachers, we practice together, the teacher dies, the student keeps on, herself a teacher by then.
So anyway, to continue our remembrance of Mel, I want to share a little piece by him too.
This is a short essay, really I think adapted from a Dharma talk, about how to sit zazen.
I thought that would be topical.
This little piece was published in the Berkeley Zen Center newsletter in 2009.
Somehow I got a copy of that paper newsletter and photocopied it.
It became one of the standard handouts that we used to give people at our center, at Red Cedar Dharma Hall.
And the article is actually from a talk Mel gave even further back, in 1983.
So there's something kind of great here about remembering Mel from stuff he wrote a long time ago.
Somehow it feels appropriate.
It's a homage to his steadiness and constancy, caring for what he received, what he learned, warm hand to warm hand from Suzuki Roshi, until this year when he died.
I don't want to trivialize: he was an intelligent man for sure.
I'm sure he had many new ideas, learned many new things, studied things, and had lots of ways that he taught.
But also I think, with him, like so many great teachers, there's this deep sense that they're basically just saying the same thing.
As long as sentient beings abide, I will say the same thing, if it helps them.
It doesn't matter to me if I'm repeating myself.
It's wonderful.
The other reason I thought it's nice to share this is that Norman mentioned Mel never published any books in his lifetime.
But this was his style of publishing, I think: a paper newsletter that gets photocopied, passed around hand to hand, getting dog-eared and worn out.
At one point ours got so worn out that we found they'd put a PDF on the internet.
Now our copies are from the PDF, so we lost that a little bit.
Anyway, here's Mel, and really listen to this because it's very practical.
Good sesshin advice for us.
It's two pages.
In sesshin, or long sitting, we say, to unify the mind, embrace the mind.
We usually, oops, sorry, I was going to [unclear: "lie a little bit"].
Let me start over, excuse me for that.
*In sesshin, or long sitting, we say, to unify the mind, or embrace the mind.
We realize the basic unity of body and mind with the whole universe.
In sesshin, the principle is to unify body, breath, and mind.
That's what we mean by embracing the mind or unifying the mind.
Mind is already one with these things.
We just need to realize it, or re-mind, or re-establish our balance and our harmony continuously.*
*It's necessary to find our balance in each moment.
What I mean by balance is to take into account and be aware of all the forces that are active in our body and mind at any given moment.
For instance, when we sit zazen, gravity is one great force acting on our body.
Another great force is what I call spirit.
It keeps our body upright.
These are the two counteracting forces, or polarities, of our life.
The pull towards the earth, and the pull away from the earth.
The earth pulls everything towards it, and so we say we're grounded on the earth.
But the counter-force of vital spirit is pulling or pushing us away from the earth, pushing us up.*
*So we're always concerned with the balance of forces between gravity and growth, or spirit.
Birth and death.
When we sit zazen the whole time, from beginning to end of our long sitting, we are dealing single-mindedly with the problem of spirit and gravity.
All of the problems that arise in between spirit and gravity are the factors of our practice.
To sit upright, not lean to the left or the right, not lean forward, not lean back.
It's that simple.
How do you just sit all day without leaning forward or backward, without leaning left or right, without moving, and remain comfortable?
We struggle with this problem.
Zazen is to struggle with this problem until, finally, we stop struggling and allow our spirit to find complete unity with gravity.
So it's a good problem, in other words.*
*What do we need to know in order to be able to deal with this problem of gravity and spirit?
Recently I've been talking about how we keep time with our chanting, how we follow the rhythm and at the same time create the rhythm and push the rhythm, how we follow and lead at the same time.
This following and leading at the same time is a koan for us.
When you can follow and lead simultaneously without any gap, then there's no following and there's no leading.
To lead is to follow and to follow is to lead.
Without losing this unity, we sometimes emphasize leading, we sometimes emphasize following.
There must always be balance in unity.
This example of chanting can be taken into every situation.*
*When we're leading the chant with the mokugyo, one necessary thing is to listen.
The other is to lead, to activate yourself.
When receiving and response is one unit without a gap, we say there's no subject and no object.
Chanting just chants, sitting just sits.
The unity illuminates subject and object.
Exhaling, we give in to gravity.
Inhaling, we reach for the sky.
In one complete breath, the unity of birth and death.*
*Zazen has two sides.
One is the passive side, the other is the active side.
The passive side corresponds to awareness, to being attentive, to just letting things come and go.
The active side is purposeful effort of body and mind, fully engaged in upright posture, total exertion and focus.
The balance of these two is what we are continuously working with.
The passive side allows for all difficulties, allows them to be here.
It is opening completely to everything, without trying to block anything, without trying to inhibit the difficulties and problems.
It's not holding anything.
The active side is the spirit of determination.
It's the form side with which we maintain our posture.
With the active side we maintain our attitude of constancy, keeping a check on our activity, returning to our original intention over and over, active and passive.*
*The passive side goes along with gravity, while the active side provides the pull away from gravity, giving us the form which allows the spirit to be fully expressed.
It's very important in sitting practice to maintain the form of posture, to maintain our focus without losing concentration.
When we put forth our total effort to maintain the form, at the same time open up completely in a passive, accepting way, then we have the perfect balance between doing and being.*
*It's the harmony between these two which accounts for our being either comfortable or uncomfortable.
Let me underline that.
It's the harmony between these two which accounts for our being comfortable or uncomfortable.
Even though we may have pain or discomfort, it doesn't succumb to suffering if we're in harmony.
Many of us cannot maintain an ideal sitting position for one reason or another.
But each of us can work within the limitations imposed by our physical formation, which is what we're all doing anyway.
So when we have this kind of experience, we can enjoy our life, which includes various difficulties.
We can still smile and help people.
It's not necessary to be a victim of our difficulties.
When we're not victims, we have freedom.
Within this most confined posture, we exist with total freedom.
This is the most stable posture in which to sit for long periods of time.
We're not trying to do anything extreme by putting our legs behind our ears.
To sit for a long period of time, this is the easiest way.*
*The unity between active and passive, between gravity and spirit, the basic unity between things is always there at the bottom.
All things share the essence.
The way is to express this harmony through zazen.
When we sit today, we should make that effort to close the gap.
Within the total activity is total stillness.
Within that stillness is total dynamic activity.
It's not I am sitting zazen, but just this sitting.*
*Putting attention on posture is most important.
How is the mudra?
Is it being held right?
Is the back correct, given our limitations?
Ears in line with the shoulders, nose in line with the navel?
Is the chest open?
Are the shoulders relaxed?
Is the breath deep?
If you battle gravity, gravity will win.
Don't fight gravity.
Come partners with it.*
*Giving to gravity what belongs to gravity.
Let your shoulders fall.
Your shoulders don't hold you up.
What kind of effort is needed to hold you up?
There is a fine line.
Where is the fine line, which is just balance?
When we find that balance, that harmony, and total effort seems effortless.*
That's the end of this little essay.
This last little line about the shoulders has stuck with me from the first time I read it: your shoulders don't hold you up.
Shoulders don't hold you up.
So beautiful encouragement from Mel about zazen as embodied practice.
Deeply embodied practice.
He talks a little bit about being so inclusive of all of our problems.
He uses the word passive in a little different way than we often use it, passive as a positive, free spaciousness.

One of the things that's interesting to me about this writing is that, just like in Dogen's essay Fukanzazengi that we chanted this morning, Mel doesn't really say that much about what to do with our minds.
Nor does Dogen.
He talks about the body and the attitude and the spirit.
Not all that much very concrete about what to do with our minds, which seems like is usually high on our minds' list of questions.
So why is that?
Are these teachers trying to tell us by implication that it's not helpful to worry too much about what's going on with our minds?
Maybe they don't want to give us too much.
The last piece about breathing that Norman shared yesterday, I think it says something about coming back to the breathing when you lose track of it.
But what do we do when our mind is just too tight, too tense?
Crazy, busy, bouncing all around, or really sluggish and out of it and lost?
We can't settle on the breath at all for one reason or another.
We're just depressed and upset.
Is there anything to do?

So you may have noticed this morning, or maybe many times, that in the Dogen piece, Fukanzazengi, his zazen instruction essay that we chant, Dogen gives us many detailed instructions about the exact physical arrangement of the room, the posture of the body, down to exactly which hand and which leg go which and where, and so on.
And then at the end of all that, almost as an aside, he quotes from a koan to give us a little hint about working with the mind.
He wrote:
*Think not thinking.
How do you think not thinking?
Non-thinking.
Think not thinking.
How do you think not thinking?
Non-thinking.*
And then, as if to sum it up, he says, *This is the essential art of zazen.* So I thought it might be interesting to take a little look at the koan behind this expression from Dogen.
If your mind is already saying, "All right, cool, now we're going to learn what it means," you can recognize that quality of mind so quick, right?
Okay, now we're going to get it.
But let's explore.
Quoting and arranging from this, as presented in his own koan collection, here's the story:
*When Master Yaoshan was sitting in meditation, a monk asked, "What do you think about sitting in steadfast composure?"
Yaoshan said, "I think not thinking."
The monk asked, "How do you think of not thinking?"
Yaoshan said, "Non-thinking."*
I'll read that again.
Punctuation there is by Truffle the Dog, by the way, if you heard that in the background.
*When Master Yaoshan was sitting in meditation, a monk asked, "What do you think about sitting there in steadfast composure?"
Yaoshan, the teacher, said, "I think not thinking."
Yaoshan said, "Non-thinking."*
So you aren't the first person to be puzzled by this.
And also to wonder, like I wondered, is there just something you lost in translation?
What possible difference is there between not thinking and non-thinking?
Not and non seem to equally just be negation.
And why do we even have these two terms?
Is one bad and the other good?
The teacher seems to be doing one of them in his zazen, not thinking, and explains, when asked how to do that, with the other, non-thinking.
So are they the same thing, actually?
Since not and non are so synonymous in English, is the negation that's used in Chinese or Japanese different?
So I found a helpful little essay.
I think I found this before.
Thank you, Google.
There's a little essay on this by a teacher named Koun Franz.
Koun Franz is a great guy.
He's an American-born Zen monk about my age, trained in Japan, and now he runs a center in Nova Scotia, Eastern Canada.
Really smart, thoughtful, reliable guy.
Fluent in Japanese.
So in his little essay, he talks about how he's been the translator for English-speaking audiences of multiple talks about this.
Japanese teachers like to talk about this story.
So he's heard lots of different explanations as he translated.
Pretty interesting way to learn.
And of course he knows the language.
So in Japanese, he tells us, the word that's being used for thinking is this word shiryu.
He says not thinking is fu shiryu and non-thinking is i shiryu.
So this word shiryu for thinking has a little sound in front of it.
One time it's fu, fu shiryu.
The other time it's i, i shiryu.
He says the fu in not thinking is a common negating prefix similar to un or non.
And the i of non-thinking is also a common negating prefix.
Really the difference between fu and i is negligible.
Okay, that clears that up.
Not and non are pretty good, paralleling the negligible difference of fu and i in Japanese anyway, and whatever the underlying Chinese characters are.
So I don't know if that really helps, but we're off the hook a little bit.
There's no real difference in the language between not thinking and non-thinking.
So it's not a translation issue.
But the really interesting thing he shares is this:
*There's one hint we can gain from language though.
And I bring it up because I've never once heard this discussed in English.
It's this word shiryu.
Shiryu, shiryu, sorry, shiryu, shiryu is not the common word for thinking.
There's other words for thinking.
Let's start with the same shi, which itself means thought.
Like shiji, shiko, shian.
But ryu is very specific.
Ryu refers to measurement.
Which means that this dialogue from the start is not about just any kind of thinking.
It's not about daydreaming.
It's not about other kinds of thinking.
It's about the aspect of mind that measures and evaluates.
That holds up a yardstick to experience, to thought objects.
It's a kind of directed thought.*
This I think is important to keep in mind.
So Dogen's not talking about just any random kind of thinking.
He's talking about evaluative thinking.
And Yaoshan was before him.
The thinking that tries to measure.
And then when you think about it that way, you notice that Dogen sprinkles Fukanzazengi with lots of pointers about this topic.
Here's one:
*Don't base it on intellectual understanding or intellectual measuring.
Pursuing words and following after speech.
Instead, learn the backward step that turns your light inwardly to illuminate yourself.*
So what is this backward step?
Turns your light.
It illuminates.
How can you inhabit that?
Practice that.
It's a wonderful sesshin question.
It's not about thinking.
It's about taking the backward step.
*The person I speak of is not learning meditation.
This isn't even meditation.
It's simply the Dharma gate of repose and bliss.
The practice realization of totally culminated enlightenment.*
So if it's not meditation, it's not an activity like that we can measure, right?
Because it's not doing something that leads to something.
It's not a technique.
It's manifestation and allowing.
Allowing of repose and bliss, he says.
Mel says we may have to grapple with the problem for a while, but then we'll feel this nature of zazen as repose and bliss.
And Dogen throws in some lofty language about enlightenment too, but let's not worry about that.
There's another way Dogen talks about it:
*It must be deportment beyond hearing and seeing.
Is it not a principle prior to knowledge and perception?*
So deportment, where you put yourself, right?
But beyond what you can see or hear or think or know, prior to your knowledge and perception.
So if this is some pre-knowledge activity, how can we judge it?
How can we try to think about it?
How can we understand it?
Dogen is very correct about the evaluative thinking too, reminding us to cut it out, about all the judging, right?
Judging whether our zazen is good or bad or we're doing a good job or not.
He wrote:
*Do not think good or bad.
Do not administer pros or cons.*
And it's very typical for Buddhism, there's a lot about what not to do.
*Intelligence or lack of it does not matter.
Between the dull and the sharp-witted there is no distinction.*
So it completely doesn't matter if this talk is making any sense to you, or if it makes any sense at all.
But I think we could really misunderstand all this too, right?
This doesn't just mean sit there and space out.
That doesn't just mean put it in park until the bell rings.
If you do that enough time, something good will happen.
There is more than that going on.
There is practice, right?
There is effort.
There's showing up.
Maybe showing up is a good way to think about this, I don't know.
We're always limited by language and concept to try and talk about this stuff.
There's a showing up for zazen.
A showing up for Buddha.
A showing up for Sangha.
A showing up so that zazen can be zazen.
And allowing.
And Mel tells us that when we really show up, our effort is to sit with care in the midst of what may appear at first to be different, maybe even to be opposite.
He talks about active and passive, gravity and spirit.
He says that our effort in zazen is to close the gap.
Close the gap between these things that we are perceiving as so different.
Maybe Dogen would encourage us to recognize, maybe to wonder, I guess, whether there was ever a gap to begin with.
And if Mel's list doesn't engage you, active and passive, gravity and spirit, notice what the apparent differences and opposites are for you.
We do this dividing up of our life and our world so automatically that we don't always notice it.
Another wonderful opportunity for zazen to notice the way we're chopping things up.
Chopping ourselves into pieces.
So it can be curious about the ways you do that.
How about, I'll just make up a few examples, but you've got to find out what this is for you.
How about me and my life?
Isn't there an odd bit of tension there?
Me and my life.
It's strange the way we would think that.
Like there's some person here, me, that has this thing called my life to manage or do something with.
Or how about, maybe this is this kind of thinking, how about how I am now and how I wish I was, how I wish I were.
We make such elaborate constructs in our mind, right?
Constructing our sense of who we are and who we wish we are.
Probably they seem really different, but are they different?
Can we close that gap?
Is there really a gap?
Or me and the world.
Me and others.
Me and other.
So many ways we separate.
Close, heal, release, soften, float away as we settle into sesshin.
So maybe this is something about what Yaoshan was on about in the eighth century.
About the non-thinking, not-thinking business, or what Dogen was riffing on in the twelfth century, or Mel was speaking about partway through the twentieth century.
And here we are, twenty-first century Zoom sesshin.
Still the same exploration that humans seem to do.
One last little translation thing before we go.
Another translation you see of non-thinking, which is Dogen's punch line in his instruction, is that maybe non-thinking actually is beyond thinking.
It appears to be pretty far from the original word, but it does sound a lot nicer to us, I think.
So listen to this.
Think not thinking.
How do you think not thinking?
Beyond thinking.
Ah, it feels good, huh?
Who doesn't want to go beyond?
And yet here we are.
We're here.
We're not beyond.
We're taking this breath.
We're feeling this body.
We're watching the light play across the room as we sit our way through the day together, each in our own room.
And yet together.
Maybe there's a beyond quality to all of this, but where would we go?
Where would beyond be?
So I think maybe the important thing for listening to all of this, maybe the important thing is just accept and accept.
Accept what happens.
Zazen as something we definitely are very involved in, right?
We're in the middle of the thing.
It's more like something we allow.
We set up and we allow zazen to be zazen, much more than something we do or figure out and we analyze and measure.
And I think the nice thing is there's a sort of a self-correcting quality to the whole thing.

Little by little, the brain inevitably gets really tired from the stress of all that shiryo, shiryo, shiryo, all that evaluative thinking, all that comparing and all the residue that builds up from all that.
Little by little the mind relaxes about it all.
It doesn't need to do it quite so much.
All of this in the middle of our breathing.
Breathing in the whole universe.
Breathing in aliveness.
Breathing in each other.
Breathing with each other.
Breathing with Mel.
Breathing with Buddha.
Just breathing in.
No gaps.
No gaps.
So thank you again.
Thank you for devoting your week to this and maybe many weeks and years to this, practicing in this forum and other forums.
Thank you for being together as Sangha, with Sangha, creating Sangha.
And I think even through the little screen here, the depth to which we support each other really can't be measured, you know.
Shiryo can try all it wants, but it can't be measured.
It's too big.
Thank you to Norman for sitting in the teacher's seat all these years.
Thank you to Mel for living your wonderful version of Suzuki Roshi's way for sixty-something years.
Thank you to Jay for your kind, wise spirit.
I wish I had gotten to spend more time with you.
I guess the last thank you is to Zoom, who will now talk to us.

verbatim.text: Thanks, everybody. I'm feeling really honored to get to speak with you this morning. So thanks in advance for sharing your attention with me. Even over Zoom, really talks are not just like broadcasts, you know, they're really co-created. Speaker and sangha are interacting, supporting each other. So thanks for that. I really appreciated Norman's remarks yesterday about our dear colleague, Jay Semino. And about his teacher, Sojun Mel Weitsman's passing this year. And it's a normal thing, actually, in our tradition to have a memorial sesshin after an important teacher dies. So it turns out that's what we're doing this year, having a memorial sesshin for Mel. And I was thinking, like, the spirit of this shouldn't only be to access whatever appreciation we might have, you know, directly or indirectly,

for Sojun Mel's practice, you know, for his incredible steadfastness, his hard work establishing a center and guiding others along the way, his unbelievable devotion to daily zazen, daily practice, showing up at the temple every day for 50, 60 years. Because all that's wonderful, but it's kind of like looking towards the past. So we only did that. We're reducing Mel to nostalgia. So it seems like the other important piece is to really inhabit our practice now. That's the memorial sesshin to show up now in our lives with the spirit inspired by the inspiration of this teacher and the many teachers. And I think a part of that might be, since we seem to be doing a memorial sesshin for Sojun Mel Weitsman over Zoom, is to not see the, you know, be careful not to see the online sesshin as, like, less than in any way, you know, but completely its own unique opportunity to practice.

So I was thinking about this because when I was coming upstairs from breakfast to get ready for the talk a little earlier, I was kind of thinking about how my kind of daily busy routine kind of pulls me out of myself. Do you know what I mean? I was actually kind of musing about this. And then my brain jumped to, my mind jumped to, as if on cue, where's my phone? It wasn't in my pocket. It was a sesshin. And it just took another half a second for my mind to imagine my phone sitting on the desk charging. And another half second I could feel kind of starting in the gut and emanating out to the limbs this urge to go check. You know, I'm talking about not just a mental urge, but a physical volitional thing. I could feel my limbs start moving in that direction.

I was just grateful for the support of sesshin. I don't think of myself as a serious smartphone addict, but it doesn't matter what I think. Maybe I am. But here's the support of our practice, you know, to be able to drop back into the breathing and move on, register that and let it go. Sit down and follow my intention.
